hero_subtitle: Traces, logs, and metrics over OpenTelemetry, powered by ClickHouse. Sub-second queries across billions of rows — or let your AI agent run them for you.
sov_title: Your data, your instrumentation, your bill.
sov_lede: Maple is the observability backend you'd build if you weren't optimizing for the invoice. OpenTelemetry in. ClickHouse speed out. The source on GitHub the whole time.
sov_pillar_1_body: Source on GitHub under FSL-1.1 — each release becomes Apache 2.0 after two years. Read every line, fork it, self-host on your own boxes if that's what your security review needs.
sov_pillar_2_body: OTLP straight in. No proprietary agent. The instrumentation you write today moves to anywhere OTel-compatible tomorrow.
sov_pillar_3_body: Pay $39/month for 100 GB per signal, then a flat $0.30/GB. No per-host fees. No per-seat fees. The pricing page and your invoice show the same numbers.
trace_title: Read the trace, not the chart.
trace_lede: Every request ends up as a span tree with attributes you can actually inspect. Hover any row in this trace to see what was on it.
logs_title: A log feed that doesn't crater your bill at scale.
logs_lede: Structured logs streamed straight from OTLP. Severity, service, message, duration. Searchable in seconds, retained for 30 days on Startup — custom retention on Enterprise.
map_lede: Live request flow across your services. Hot services light up. The cascade you'd otherwise reconstruct from a postmortem is right here in the foreground.
mcp_title: Your AI agent reads it too.
mcp_lede: Maple ships with a first-class MCP server. Any compatible agent can list services, search traces, find errors, and propose fixes. The transcript on the right walks through the exact tool calls an agent makes.
mcp_point_1_title: Reads the code, not just the trace
mcp_point_1_body: The agent pulls the source file behind a span, so the fix it proposes cites your actual code.
mcp_point_2_body: Claim an issue, set its severity, attach a fix. Not a read-only dashboard.
mcp_point_3_body: Point any MCP client at the endpoint and sign in. Open protocol, nothing to install.
sessions_lede: Session replay with every click, route, console line, and failed request captured. Replay and your spans share one session id — so you jump from the moment it broke straight to the trace behind it.
k8s_title: The pod underneath the slow span.
k8s_lede: Drop a Helm chart on your cluster. Kubelet, host, and kube-state metrics start flowing in. Every span your apps emit arrives carrying pod, node, and namespace, so a slow request lands you on the exact replica that served it.
bill_lede: Side by side, at list price. The questions your finance team will ask, answered before they have to ask.
bill_footnote: Competitor cells summarize public list prices — check each vendor's pricing page for current numbers. Maple's rate is the published flat per-GB. Use the calculator to project your monthly cost.
cta_bookend_lede: 14-day free trial, card required, no charge until it ends. Self-hosting is supported, and `maple start` needs no account at all.
footer_manifesto: No per-seat fees. No proprietary agents. No black boxes.
trustbar_text: Works with every language OpenTelemetry supports
product_heading: One platform for all your observability data
product_subtitle: From high-level service health to individual span attributes — everything in one place.
features_heading: The debugging workflow, end to end
features_tracing_desc: Visualize request flows across services with flamegraph and waterfall views. Drill into any span to see attributes, events, and timing.
features_logs_desc: Search and filter logs with full-text search. Correlated with traces for seamless debugging across your stack.
features_metrics_desc: Track request rates, error rates, and latency percentiles. Build custom charts from any metric your services emit.
features_service_heading: All your services at a glance
features_service_desc: See all your services at a glance with latency percentiles, throughput, error rates, and environment badges.
features_errors_heading: Group, track, and fix errors systematically
features_errors_desc: Errors are automatically grouped by type across all your services. See trends over time, affected services, and drill into sample traces to find the root cause.
usecases_ecommerce_heading: Checkout errors spike during a flash sale
usecases_ecommerce_desc: Your flash sale goes live and payment failures start climbing. You need to find the failing service, the exact error, and the upstream cause — fast.
usecases_ecommerce_result: In this scenario: a Stripe timeout, correlated with retry-exhaustion logs — root cause in about 90 seconds.
usecases_microservices_heading: API latency doubles without any deployment
usecases_microservices_desc: No one deployed anything, but P95 latency just doubled. The service map shows which dependency is the bottleneck and how the cascade propagates.
usecases_microservices_result: Service map reveals connection pool exhaustion cascading from user-db.
usecases_ai_desc: An alert fires at 3 AM. Before your on-call is fully awake, an MCP agent connects to Maple, investigates the spike, and posts what it found to Slack.
usecases_ai_result: In this scenario, the agent posts its diagnosis to #incidents before anyone wakes up.
usecases_diagnosis_text: Stripe API timeout causing payment failures. Connection pool at capacity. Recommend circuit breaker activation.
otel_heading: Built on the standard, not around it
otel_vendor_desc: Your instrumentation works with any OTel-compatible backend. Switch providers without changing a line of application code.
otel_future_desc: Backed by every major cloud provider. OpenTelemetry graduated from the CNCF in 2026 and is its second most active project after Kubernetes.
otel_signals_desc: Traces, logs, and metrics from one SDK — no separate vendor agents to install and reconcile per signal.
otel_community_desc: Thousands of contributors and auto-instrumentation for most major frameworks. The spec is driven by the community, not one vendor's roadmap.
tech_columnar_desc: A columnar engine built for telemetry. Scans billions of rows and returns in well under a second — no pre-aggregation required.
tech_correlated_desc: Jump from a trace to its logs, from a log to its metric. Every signal is connected by trace and span IDs.
tech_realtime_desc: Data is queryable within seconds of ingestion. No waiting for batch jobs or delayed indexes.
tech_connectors_desc: Pull data from Cloudflare Logpush and Prometheus scrape targets alongside your OpenTelemetry signals.
ai_heading: Let an AI agent run the investigation
ai_desc: Maple has a built-in MCP server and AI agent that query your traces, logs, errors, and metrics directly. Connect any MCP-compatible client and let agents investigate production issues and propose fixes.
ai_alert_threshold: Error rate for api-gateway exceeded 5% threshold
ai_investigating: Investigating the error spike. Let me check system health first.
ai_above_threshold: Error rate is at 8.4%, well above threshold. Let me find the specific errors.
ai_inspecting: 142 ConnectionTimeout errors. Inspecting a trace to find the root cause.
ai_root_cause: Root cause: db.query span is timing out in the users service. The database connection pool is exhausted.
chat_heading: Ask your telemetry in plain language
chat_desc: A built-in AI assistant that understands your traces, logs, and metrics. Ask questions in plain language and get answers with direct links to the relevant data.
chat_user_msg: What caused the latency spike on payment-service in the last hour?
chat_response_1: I found a latency spike starting at 14:12 UTC. The P95 jumped from 140ms to 890ms.
chat_response_2: Root cause: 3 slow database queries in the checkout flow averaging 720ms each. The connection pool hit its max limit (20/20).
dashboard_heading: Build dashboards that tell the story
dashboard_desc: Drag-and-drop widgets, pick from pre-built presets, or let AI suggest the right charts for your services. Export and share as JSON.
dashboard_ai_text: Add a P95 latency chart for payment-service
alert_rules_desc: 7 built-in signal types — error rate, P95/P99 latency, Apdex, throughput, custom metrics, and custom queries. With severity levels, incident tracking, and auto-resolution.
alert_route_desc: Push alerts to Slack, Discord, PagerDuty, or any webhook. Your team gets notified where they already work.
how_step1_desc: Add the OpenTelemetry SDK to your app. Auto-instrumentation handles the rest.
how_step2_desc: Point the OTLP exporter at Maple. Traces, logs, and metrics flow automatically.
how_step3_desc: Open the dashboard and start exploring. Everything is queryable, filterable, and fast.
bottomcta_subtitle: Add the SDK, point OTLP at Maple, and watch traces arrive — most setups take under five minutes.
footer_tagline: Open-source observability platform built on OpenTelemetry.
pricing_trial_reassure: Free for {duration} days · Cancel anytime · Card required to start
pricing_enterprise_rail: Higher volume, custom retention, priority support.
pricing_calc_sub: Slide your monthly volume and compare your Maple cost against any vendor.
faq_ingestion_a: Maple measures ingestion by the volume of data you send — logs, traces, and metrics are each measured in gigabytes. Each plan includes a monthly data allowance per signal type. Check the plans above for exact limits.
faq_limits_q: What happens if I exceed my plan limits?
faq_limits_a: We'll notify you as you approach your included volume. On the Startup plan, additional usage is billed at a flat $0.30 per GB — the same rate shown on this page.
faq_retention_a: Retention varies by plan — the Startup plan includes 30-day retention and Enterprise plans offer custom retention periods. All plans include full query access to your retained data.
faq_otel_a: Yes — Maple is built natively on OpenTelemetry. Any application instrumented with OTel SDKs or the OTel Collector can send data directly to Maple with zero code changes. No proprietary agents required.
faq_selfhost_a: Yes. Maple's source is available under FSL-1.1 (each release becomes Apache 2.0 after two years), and the project can be self-hosted on your own infrastructure. The cloud plan is available for teams that prefer a managed experience.
faq_trial_q: Do you offer a free trial for paid plans?
faq_trial_a: The Startup plan includes a 14-day free trial. A credit card is required, and you won't be charged until the trial ends. Enterprise plans start with a conversation instead.
page_home_title: Open Source Observability for Traces, Logs & Metrics · Maple
page_home_desc: Open-source observability platform built on OpenTelemetry. Collect, visualize, and analyze distributed traces, logs, and metrics from your services with AI-powered diagnostics.
page_pricing_desc: Transparent usage-based pricing for logs, traces, and metrics. No per-seat fees, no hidden costs.
page_pricing_subtitle: Usage-based pricing with no per-seat fees and no hidden costs. 14-day free trial on the Startup plan.
page_otel_desc: Maple is built natively on OpenTelemetry. Ingest traces, logs, and metrics via OTLP with full spec compliance — no proprietary agents, no vendor lock-in.
page_otel_heading: Built on OpenTelemetry from the ground up
page_otel_subtitle: Maple is a fully OTel-native observability platform. Every signal — traces, logs, and metrics — flows through the open standard. No proprietary agents, no SDK lock-in.
page_otel_what_is_p1: OpenTelemetry is the CNCF open-source standard for collecting observability data from distributed systems. It provides a single, vendor-neutral set of APIs, SDKs, and tools to instrument your applications and export traces, logs, and metrics.
page_otel_what_is_p2: With support for every major language and framework, OTel has become the industry default for telemetry instrumentation — backed by contributions from hundreds of organizations.
page_otel_no_vendor_desc: Your instrumentation stays the same regardless of which backend you choose. Switch providers without touching application code.
page_otel_one_standard_desc: Traces, logs, and metrics share a unified data model with correlated context. No stitching together separate tools.
page_otel_community_desc: Backed by the CNCF and hundreds of contributors. The spec evolves with real-world needs, not a single vendor's roadmap.
page_otel_language_desc: First-party SDKs for Go, Java, Python, JavaScript, .NET, Rust, and more. Auto-instrumentation available for most frameworks.
page_otel_future_desc: As the industry converges on OTel, your investment in instrumentation carries forward. No more rip-and-replace migrations.
page_otel_ecosystem_desc: Collectors, exporters, processors, and connectors — a full pipeline you can customize to match your infrastructure.
page_otel_spec_otlp_desc: Send telemetry directly via OTLP/gRPC or OTLP/HTTP. No translation layers, no proprietary formats.
page_otel_spec_semantic_desc: Maple understands and indexes OTel semantic conventions — HTTP, database, RPC, messaging — out of the box.
page_otel_spec_signals_desc: First-class support for traces, logs, and metrics. Each signal is stored, queried, and correlated natively.
page_otel_spec_collector_desc: Use the OpenTelemetry Collector to route, filter, and batch telemetry before sending it to Maple.
page_otel_spec_sdk_desc: Works with every official OTel SDK. If it speaks OTLP, Maple can ingest it — no vendor-specific libraries required.
page_otel_spec_context_desc: W3C Trace Context and Baggage propagation supported. Correlate spans, logs, and metrics across service boundaries.
page_otel_ecosystem_heading: Works with your existing OTel setup
page_otel_ecosystem_p1: Already using the OpenTelemetry Collector, auto-instrumentation agents, or OTel SDKs? Point your OTLP exporter at Maple and start seeing data immediately. No code changes, no new agents to deploy.
page_otel_ecosystem_p2: Maple fits into the OTel ecosystem as a backend — receiving, storing, and visualizing the telemetry your existing pipeline produces. Swap in Maple without disrupting your instrumentation.
page_roadmap_desc: See what we're building, what's in progress, and what's shipped. Maple's development roadmap is transparent and updated regularly.
page_roadmap_subtitle: A transparent view of Maple's development. See what's shipped, what's in progress, and where we're headed next.
page_bs_desc: See what your users actually did, then jump straight to the trace behind it. Full session replay with clicks, console, network, and errors on one timeline.
page_bs_heading: Watch the session. Jump to the trace.
page_bs_subtitle: See exactly what the user did — every navigation, click, console line, network call, and error — each one tagged with the trace it triggered. Replay and your backend share one session id, so a single click takes you from what they saw to why it broke.
page_bs_timeline_desc: Every navigation, click, input, console line, network call, and error in one ordered stream you can scrub through.
page_bs_replay_desc: Watch the session play back exactly as the user experienced it — every scroll, input, and state change.
page_bs_correlation_desc: Replay and spans share one session id. Jump from any moment on screen to the exact trace behind it.
page_bs_capture_desc: Console logs and network requests with status codes, recorded inline — so you see the failure, not just the symptom.
page_bs_errors_desc: Exceptions and rejections land on the timeline right next to the actions that led up to them.
page_bs_privacy_desc: Mask inputs and text before anything leaves the browser. Tune sampling and redaction in a single line of setup.
page_dt_desc: Visualize request flows across services with flamegraph and waterfall views. Drill into any span to see attributes, events, and timing.
page_dt_subtitle: Visualize request flows with flamegraph, waterfall, and flow views. See exactly where time is spent across your distributed system.
page_dt_waterfall_view_desc: See the full timeline of a request with nested spans, timing bars, and service colors.
page_dt_flamegraph_desc: Identify hot paths and time-consuming operations with interactive flamegraph visualization.
page_dt_flow_desc: Understand service-to-service communication with an interactive dependency flow diagram.
page_dt_attributes_desc: Inspect HTTP headers, database queries, error messages, and custom attributes on any span.
page_dt_correlation_desc: Jump from any span directly to its correlated logs. Every signal connected by trace ID.
page_dt_filtering_desc: Filter traces by service, duration, status, HTTP method, and custom attributes.
page_k8s_desc: Monitor Kubernetes clusters with OpenTelemetry. A Helm chart collects kubelet, host, and kube-state metrics; spans arrive enriched with pod, node, and namespace.
page_k8s_heading: Cluster, workload, and span in one view
page_k8s_subtitle: Install one Helm chart. Kubelet, host, and kube-state metrics flow in over OTLP. The OpenTelemetry Operator injects pod identity into every span your apps emit, so a slow request lands you on the exact replica that served it.
page_k8s_helm: Helm chart, not a black box
page_k8s_helm_desc: maple-k8s-infra is a small Helm chart you can read end-to-end. Kubelet stats per pod, host metrics per node, kube-state metrics across the cluster. OTLP receivers on every node for your apps.
page_k8s_correlation_desc: Spans arrive carrying k8s.pod.name, k8s.node.name, and k8s.namespace.name. Drill from a slow trace straight to the pod and node that ran it.
page_k8s_kube_state_desc: Deployments, StatefulSets, DaemonSets, replica counts, and pod phase, all scraped via the standard kube-state-metrics exporter.
page_k8s_views_desc: Three first-class infrastructure views in the dashboard. Inspect a deployment, a single pod, or a single node, with the same filters you use everywhere else.
page_k8s_operator_desc: Pods get OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT and pod/node identity injected at admission. Apps with an OTel SDK linked are instrumented without code changes.
page_k8s_multi_desc: One ingest endpoint per organization. Send from prod, staging, and a developer's kind cluster, and split them with cluster-name resource attributes.
page_k8s_console_title: Workloads, pods, and nodes — one filter sidebar
page_k8s_console_lede: The same view your platform team lives in. Facet down to a deployment in a namespace on a node, or scope to a cluster and watch it live.
page_k8s_workloads_subtitle: Aggregated pod metrics by deployment, statefulset, and daemonset.
page_k8s_views_lede: Same filters everywhere. Click through from a workload to its pods to the node that runs them.
page_k8s_views_pods_lede: Per-pod CPU and memory — against requests and limits.
page_k8s_views_nodes_lede: Kubelet stats per node, with uptime and lifecycle.
page_k8s_correlation_title: From a slow span to the exact pod
page_k8s_correlation_lede: The OpenTelemetry Operator stamps every span with k8s.pod.name, k8s.node.name, and k8s.namespace.name at admission. The slow trace already knows where it ran.
page_k8s_install_lede: Read the chart end-to-end. Three commands and the cluster is reporting kubelet, host, and kube-state metrics over OTLP.
page_dd_title: Datadog Alternative (Open Source) — Maple vs Datadog
page_dd_desc: Compare Maple and Datadog for observability. Maple offers transparent usage-based pricing, native OpenTelemetry support, and AI-powered diagnostics — open source.
page_dd_subtitle: Datadog is powerful but comes with per-host pricing and proprietary agents. Maple covers distributed tracing, logs, and metrics with a flat per-GB rate, native OpenTelemetry ingest, and source you can read and self-host.
page_dd_transparent_desc: Simple usage-based pricing with no per-host fees, no hidden costs, and no surprise bills at the end of the month.
page_dd_otel_desc: Built on OpenTelemetry from the start. No proprietary agents to install or maintain — the OTel instrumentation you already have points straight at Maple.
page_dd_ai_desc: Diagnose issues faster with AI-powered root cause analysis and MCP tool integration for automated observability workflows.
page_dd_oss_desc: The source is on GitHub under FSL-1.1, converting to Apache 2.0 over time. Inspect every line, contribute features, and see exactly how your data is handled.
page_dd_nolock_desc: Your data stays in open formats. Switch providers or self-host at any time — your instrumentation never needs to change.
page_dd_selfhost_desc: Run Maple on your own infrastructure for complete data sovereignty, compliance, and cost control.
page_dash0_title: Dash0 Alternative (Open Source) — Maple vs Dash0
page_dash0_desc: Compare Maple and Dash0 for observability. Both are OpenTelemetry-native with transparent pricing and an MCP integration — Maple adds open source, self-hosting, and full control over your data.
page_dash0_subtitle: Dash0 and Maple are both OpenTelemetry-native with transparent usage-based pricing and no per-seat fees. The difference is ownership: Maple is open source and self-hostable, so you can run it on your own infrastructure — including your own ClickHouse — for full data sovereignty and retention control, instead of a closed SaaS backend.
page_dash0_oss_desc: Maple's source is available under the Functional Source License (FSL-1.1) — inspect every line, contribute features, and trust there are no black boxes. Dash0's backend is closed-source SaaS.
page_dash0_selfhost_desc: Run Maple on your own infrastructure for data residency and compliance. Dash0 is SaaS-only, so your telemetry has to live in their cloud.
page_dash0_retention_desc: Self-hosting puts you in control of retention and storage — keep data as long as your compliance and debugging workflows require, instead of fixed SaaS windows.
page_dash0_sovereignty_desc: Keep telemetry inside your own infrastructure for sovereignty and compliance — no third-party cloud sees your data unless you choose the hosted version.
page_dash0_clickhouse_desc: Maple's query engine speaks ClickHouse, so a self-hosted deployment can run on a ClickHouse instance you operate and scale yourself.
page_dash0_migrate_desc: Both platforms ingest standard OTLP, so moving your telemetry is just re-pointing your OpenTelemetry Collector exporter — no instrumentation changes. (Dashboards and alerts are recreated in Maple.)
page_ecommerce_desc: Debug checkout failures, payment timeouts, and inventory issues in real-time with distributed tracing and log correlation.
page_ecommerce_subtitle: When your flash sale hits and payments start failing, Maple shows you exactly what's happening across every service.
page_ecommerce_step1_desc: Your monitoring detects an error rate spike on the payment service. The alert includes the threshold breach and affected service, giving you immediate context.
page_ecommerce_step2_desc: Click into a failing trace to see the full request path. The payment span is immediately visible in red, showing a 5000ms timeout on the Stripe API call.
page_ecommerce_step3_desc: Jump to correlated logs for the failing span. The Stripe API timeout and retry exhaustion are immediately visible, confirming the root cause without switching tools.
page_ecommerce_cap_tracing_desc: Follow checkout requests from cart to payment to confirmation. See every service hop with timing.
page_ecommerce_cap_logs_desc: Every failed payment links to its retry logs and timeout errors. One click from trace to logs.
page_ecommerce_cap_errors_desc: Group payment errors by type, see trends, fix systematically. No more searching through log files.
page_nextjs_desc: Add distributed tracing, logging, and metrics to your Next.js app in minutes. Built on OpenTelemetry with zero vendor lock-in.
page_nextjs_subtitle: Add distributed tracing to your Next.js application in minutes. Capture server components, API routes, and middleware spans automatically with Vercel's built-in instrumentation hook.
faq_home_what_a: Maple is an observability platform for traces, logs, and metrics, built on OpenTelemetry and backed by ClickHouse. It lets you collect, visualize, and query telemetry from distributed systems in real time — or let an AI agent do it for you over MCP.
faq_home_oss_a: Maple's source is on GitHub under the Functional Source License (FSL-1.1) — you can read every line, fork it, and self-host. Each release becomes Apache 2.0 two years after publication. You own your data and your instrumentation, and you can run Maple yourself or use the hosted version.
faq_home_otel_a: Yes. Maple is built on OpenTelemetry — the open, vendor-neutral standard for telemetry — so there are no proprietary agents and no lock-in. If you already emit OpenTelemetry data, you can point it at Maple without re-instrumenting your code.
faq_home_price_a: The Startup plan is $39/month with 100 GB of logs, traces, and metrics each included, then a flat $0.30 per GB. No per-host or per-seat fees. Enterprise plans add custom volume and retention.
faq_home_agents_q: Does Maple work with AI agents?
faq_home_agents_a: Yes. Maple ships a first-class MCP (Model Context Protocol) server, so compatible AI agents can list services, search traces, find errors, and propose fixes directly against your telemetry.
hero_announce_text: Maple Local — the whole platform as one binary.
signals_trace_sub: Every request is a span tree with its attributes intact. Hover a row; see what was on it.
signals_logs_sub: Structured logs straight from OTLP. Severity, service, message, duration — searchable in seconds.
signals_session_sub: Every click, route, console line, and failed request. Replay and spans share one session id.
incident_title: From a 3 AM page to the line that caused it.
incident_lede: Four surfaces, one trace id. Nothing to stitch, no second tool, no tab you forgot you had open.
incident_step_1_body: Error rate on api-gateway crosses 5%. The alert carries the service, the threshold it broke, and the sample traces — not a number and a shrug. Route it to Slack, Discord, PagerDuty, or any webhook.
incident_step_2_title: The trace opens on the failing span.
incident_step_2_body: The failing request is a span tree with every attribute intact. Three Stripe retries sit at the bottom, red, each timing out at exactly 1.75 seconds. No sampling gap, no aggregate hiding the outlier.
incident_step_3_body: Jump from the failing span to its logs on the trace id. Retry exhaustion, connection pool at 20/20 — the confirmation, not a second search in a second product.
incident_step_4_title: Or hand all three steps to an agent.
incident_step_4_body: Maple ships a first-class MCP server. Point Claude, Cursor, or any MCP client at it: it lists services, searches traces, finds the errors, reads the source, and proposes the fix.
platform_title: Everything else you'd have bought separately.
platform_lede: Metrics, service maps, error grouping, alerting, and an MCP server. One platform, one instrumentation, one bill.
platform_metrics_desc: Request rate, error rate, latency percentiles. Drag the widgets yourself, or let the agent suggest the board.
platform_map_desc: Live request flow across your services. The cascade you'd otherwise reconstruct from a postmortem, in the foreground.
platform_errors_desc: Errors grouped by type across every service, with trends over time, affected services, and sample traces attached.
platform_alerts_desc: Seven signal types with severity, incident tracking, and auto-resolution. Slack, Discord, PagerDuty, or any webhook.
platform_mcp_desc: Any MCP-compatible client can list services, search traces, read the source, and propose a fix. Open protocol, no plugin.
platform_cloud_desc: Kubernetes ships as a Helm chart. PlanetScale, Cloudflare, and the rest connect in one OAuth click.
sov_pillar_4_body: Run Maple on your own infrastructure, against a ClickHouse you operate and scale yourself. Your telemetry never has to leave your network — retention and residency are your call, not a fixed SaaS window.
local_title: The whole platform, as one binary.
local_body: One Bun-compiled maple executable — OTLP ingest, an embedded ClickHouse, a query API, and the dashboard — running on 127.0.0.1. No account, no cloud, no rate limits.
pricing_home_title: Priced the way you'd price it.
pricing_home_lede: No per-host fees. No per-seat fees. The pricing page and your invoice show the same numbers.
hero_shot_overview_line: See every service at a glance.
hero_shot_traces_line: Follow one request end to end.
page_cta_lede: One endpoint, one key. Traces, logs, metrics and sessions land on the same trace id from the first request.
feat_tracing_seo_desc: Open one trace and read where the time went — waterfall, flamegraph and service flow over the same spans, with every attribute the SDK sent.
feat_tracing_hero_lede: A trace is one request laid out end to end. Maple keeps every span the SDK sent, with its attributes, its parent, and its exact millisecond offset — so a slow request stops being a guess.
feat_tracing_panel_lede: Select any span and its full attribute set opens beside the waterfall — the SQL it ran, the status it returned, the pod it ran on. Nothing is summarised away.
feat_tracing_cap_title: Four ways to read the same spans
feat_tracing_cap_1_body: Spans nested by parent, bars scaled to the trace's own duration. A 1.24 s request with a 480 ms child reads as a shape before you read a number.
feat_tracing_cap_2_body: The same spans stacked by depth instead of time. Fifty sibling db.query spans at one level is an N+1, and it is visible as a wall rather than a list.
feat_tracing_cap_3_body: The trace collapsed to the services it crossed and the calls between them. Use it when the question is which boundary, not which line.
feat_tracing_cap_4_body: Every key the SDK sent, stored as sent. db.statement, http.status_code, exception.type and your own custom keys are all queryable, not just displayable.
feat_tracing_cap_5_body: Spans and logs carry the same trace id, so any span opens the log lines written while it was running. No timestamp arithmetic across two tools.
feat_tracing_artifact_title: The real flamegraph, on a real trace
feat_tracing_artifact_lede: This is the component the product renders, running on a fixture trace. Hover a span to read its service, duration and share of the total.
feat_sessions_seo_desc: Watch the session the user actually had, then open the trace behind any moment in it. Replay, console, network and spans share one session id.
feat_sessions_hero_title: Watch it happen, then open the trace
feat_sessions_hero_lede: A replay shows you what the user did. The trace under it shows you why it failed. Both carry the same session id, so the jump between them is one click, not a reconstruction.
feat_sessions_panel_title: The recording and the evidence, side by side
feat_sessions_panel_lede: The viewport plays back exactly as rendered, with console lines, network requests and thrown exceptions on the same timeline as the clicks that caused them.
feat_sessions_cap_1_body: Navigations, clicks, inputs, console lines, network calls and errors land in one ordered stream. Each row carries the trace id that was live when it happened.
feat_sessions_cap_2_body: The DOM is recorded, not the screen. Scroll position, hover state and mid-typing input values play back as the user left them, at any window size.
feat_sessions_cap_3_title: From a moment to a span
feat_sessions_cap_3_body: Pause on the failed click and open the request it fired. The replay and the waterfall are two views of one session id, not two products stitched by timestamp.
feat_sessions_cap_4_body: Requests are recorded with method, status and duration. A 500 on POST /checkout shows up in the stream at the second it returned, not in a separate tab.
feat_sessions_cap_5_body: Inputs and text nodes are masked in the browser, before anything is sent. Sampling rate and redaction rules are config, not a support request.
feat_sessions_artifact_lede: The cursor travels to Pay now, the click lands, and the event stream fills in beside it — each entry carrying the trace id it belongs to.
feat_logs_seo_desc: Search structured logs across every service, filter by severity and resource attribute, and open the trace that produced any line.
feat_logs_hero_title: Search the logs, keep the trace
feat_logs_hero_lede: Logs arrive structured, with their resource attributes and their trace id intact. That means a search result is not a dead end — every line opens the request that wrote it.
feat_logs_panel_title: Severity, service and attribute, in one filter rail
feat_logs_panel_lede: Facets are computed from the rows actually in range, so the counts beside each severity are the counts you are about to see, not a stale summary.
feat_logs_cap_title: What you can ask of a log line
feat_logs_cap_1_title: Search the body and the attributes
feat_logs_cap_1_body: Resource and log attributes are columns, not a blob. Filter on service.name, deployment.environment or your own keys the same way you filter on the message text.
feat_logs_cap_2_body: The six OTel severity levels keep their own colour and their own facet. WARN and ERROR are one click apart, and neither is buried in a text match.
feat_logs_cap_3_title: Open the trace behind the line
feat_logs_cap_3_body: Any line carrying a trace id opens its request, positioned at the span that was running when the line was written.
feat_logs_cap_4_body: The histogram above the results is stacked by severity, so a burst of ERROR at 14:20 is visible before you have read a single line.
feat_logs_cap_5_title: Sent the way OTel defines it
feat_logs_cap_5_body: Logs come in over OTLP alongside traces and metrics. No log-shipping agent, no second pipeline to keep alive, no separate retention to reason about.
feat_logs_artifact_lede: Lines arrive as they are written, each one tagged with its service and severity. This is the tail view, and it is the same rows the search returns.
feat_metrics_seo_desc: Browse every metric your services emit, then build dashboards on the same warehouse the trace list reads from — so a chart and a trace can never disagree.
feat_metrics_hero_title: Charts that read the same data as the traces
feat_metrics_hero_lede: Every widget queries the same warehouse the trace list does. When a dashboard shows p99 at 380 ms, the traces behind that number are one click away and they agree.
feat_metrics_panel_title: Every metric, with its type and its cardinality
feat_metrics_panel_lede: The explorer lists what your services actually emit, not what a template expects. Cardinality is shown per metric, because that is the number that decides what a query costs.
feat_metrics_cap_1_body: p50, p95 and p99 on one axis, each on its own percentile colour. Latency charts use the percentile tokens, so p99 is the same red-orange everywhere in the product.
feat_metrics_cap_2_body: A single scalar with the line it must stay under. Apdex against its target, error rate against its budget — the comparison is part of the widget, not a note beside it.
feat_metrics_cap_3_body: Declare $service or $env once and every widget on the board follows the selector. One dashboard covers twelve services instead of twelve dashboards drifting apart.
feat_metrics_cap_4_body: Group-by suggestions come from the attributes that metric actually carries, so you cannot build a chart that groups by a key nothing emits.
feat_metrics_cap_5_body: Select a range on any latency chart and open the traces inside it. The chart is an index into the spans, not a picture of them.
feat_metrics_artifact_lede: Sixty five-minute buckets stacked by level. The warn cluster and the error blip after it are the shape a stat tile would have flattened away.
feat_catalog_seo_desc: Every service with its latency percentiles, error rate and throughput, and a live map of who calls whom — both built from spans, not from a config file.
feat_catalog_hero_title: The map draws itself from the spans
feat_catalog_hero_lede: There is no topology to declare. Maple reads parent-child relationships out of the traces you already send, so a new service appears on the map the first time it is called.
feat_catalog_panel_lede: Latency percentiles, error rate and throughput per service, over the range you picked. Sort by p99 and the row that needs you is the top row.
feat_catalog_cap_1_body: Every line between two nodes is a parent-child span pair that actually happened, carrying its own request rate and error rate. Nothing on the map is declared.
feat_catalog_cap_2_body: Client spans become nodes, so Postgres, Redis and every third-party API sit on the map beside your own services with the same latency columns.
feat_catalog_cap_3_body: Focus a node and the map collapses to what it talks to. A forty-service estate becomes the six services that matter to the question you are asking.
feat_catalog_cap_4_body: Each service holds one of sixteen hues, and holds it everywhere — the map, the waterfall, the charts. Colour means which service, never how healthy.
feat_catalog_cap_5_body: A service's detail view marks releases against its latency, so a step change lines up with the version that introduced it instead of a hunch.
feat_catalog_artifact_lede: Each node carries its request rate, error rate and average latency. The flow along an edge is that edge's traffic, not decoration.
feat_errors_seo_desc: Exceptions grouped into issues by type and normalised message, each one linked to the span that threw it and the release that introduced it.
feat_errors_hero_lede: Exceptions are grouped by what they are, not by how many times they happened. Each issue keeps its first occurrence, its latest, and the span that threw every one of them.
feat_errors_panel_lede: The list is issues, not events — each row carrying its type, the services it hits, its count over the range and when it was last seen.
feat_errors_cap_title: From an issue to a fix
feat_errors_cap_1_body: ConnectionTimeout out of payment-svc is one issue, not 142 events. The fingerprint is exception.type plus the message with ids, timestamps and hosts normalised out.
feat_errors_cap_2_body: An error is an event on a span, so every issue opens the trace it belongs to — with the arguments, the query and the status code that were live at the time.
feat_errors_cap_3_body: Issues carry first-seen and last-seen, so a regression reads differently from a first appearance. A resolved issue that fires again reopens rather than starting over.
feat_errors_cap_4_body: Claim an issue, set its severity, leave the note. State and comments live with the issue, so the next person on call reads what you already ruled out.
feat_errors_cap_5_body: A detector runs every five minutes and sets a severity from the issue's own rate and spread. Manual severity always wins over the detector's, and the detector's over the AI's.
feat_mcp_seo_desc: Maple ships an MCP server, so Claude Code and any other MCP client can read your traces, logs and metrics and work an incident with the same tools you do.
feat_mcp_hero_title: Give the agent the same tools you use
feat_mcp_hero_lede: The MCP server exposes the product's own queries — find_slow_traces, diagnose_service, search_logs — over an open protocol. Read-only by default, and scoped to one org.
feat_mcp_panel_lede: Point Claude Code, or anything else that speaks MCP, at the endpoint on this page. Tools are the same queries the dashboard runs, against the same warehouse.
feat_mcp_cap_title: What an agent can actually do
feat_mcp_cap_1_body: diagnose_service reads p99 by service.version, error rate and throughput over a window and returns what changed, not a chart image the model has to squint at.
feat_mcp_cap_2_body: find_slow_traces and inspect_trace return real spans with real attributes. The agent reads db.statement, not a summary of it.
feat_mcp_cap_3_body: Link a repository and search_source_code plus read_source_file let the agent get from a stack frame to the function, so its proposal cites a line rather than a guess.
feat_mcp_cap_4_body: Claiming an issue, setting a severity or opening an alert rule are separate write tools. Read-only is the default posture, and mutations need approval.
feat_mcp_cap_5_body: Every tool call is filtered by the org on the key, in the query itself. An agent cannot read across a tenant boundary because the query it runs cannot express it.
feat_mcp_artifact_lede: Five tool calls from list_services to propose_fix. Every step is a query you could have run yourself, which is why the answer is checkable.
uc_api_seo_desc: An SLO breach, traced to the release that caused it. Follow checkout p99 from the alert through the dashboard to the commit that took it from 120 ms to 380 ms.
uc_api_hero_title: The p99 moved. Find out which release moved it.
uc_api_hero_lede: An SLO is only useful if a breach points somewhere. This one goes from a threshold crossing to the commit that caused it in three surfaces, without leaving the same time range.
uc_api_story_title: Threshold to commit, in three minutes
uc_api_story_lede: One SLO holds the whole path together: checkout p99 at or under 200 ms. Every surface below is filtered to the window where it stopped being true.
uc_api_step_1_title: The alert states the breach, not the symptom
uc_api_step_1_body: The rule is written against the SLO, so the notification carries the threshold, the observed value and the evaluation window. 380 ms against 200 ms, sustained across three windows.
uc_api_step_2_title: The dashboard narrows it to one endpoint
uc_api_step_2_body: p50 has not moved. p99 has. That shape means a slow tail on one route rather than a service-wide slowdown, and the route breakdown names it: POST /checkout.
uc_api_step_3_body: Split the same endpoint by service.version and the step change has an owner: p99 120 ms on abc123, 380 ms on def456. The traces under def456 carry 50 db.query spans where the earlier ones carry 3.
uc_api_outcome_line: Reverted def456 at T+9:20. p99 back under the threshold on the next evaluation window.
uc_api_cap_1_title: The alert knows its own SLO
uc_api_cap_1_body: Rules are written against a percentile and a threshold, so a firing alert already contains the comparison. Nothing has to be looked up to know how far out it is.
uc_api_cap_2_title: Version is an attribute, so it is a filter
uc_api_cap_2_body: service.version rides on every span the SDK sends. Comparing two releases is a group-by, not an export into a spreadsheet.
uc_api_cap_3_body: p99 is computed from spans that are still there. Selecting the spike on the chart opens the requests inside it, so the number and the evidence are never separate artifacts.
uc_ecom_seo_desc: Checkout failures during a flash sale, traced from the alert to the Stripe timeout and the retry-exhaustion logs behind it — one order id the whole way.
uc_ecom_hero_title: Checkout is failing. Which orders, and why.
uc_ecom_hero_lede: During a sale, an error rate is not the question — the question is which customers lost their basket and what stopped them. One order id carries the answer across all three surfaces.
uc_ecom_story_title: One order, from the alert to the timeout
uc_ecom_story_lede: order_8421 is a real order that failed. Every surface below is filtered to it, so nothing has to be matched up by timestamp between two tools.
uc_ecom_step_1_title: The alert fires on the checkout route only
uc_ecom_step_1_body: Error rate on POST /checkout crosses its threshold while the rest of the site holds. That scoping is the first fact: this is not the sale traffic, it is the payment path.
uc_ecom_step_2_body: Open one failed order and the waterfall is unambiguous. Three retries sit at the bottom, red, each timing out at exactly 1.75 s — the client's own deadline, not the provider's.
uc_ecom_step_3_title: The logs say the pool was empty
uc_ecom_step_3_body: The lines written during those spans carry the same trace id. Retry budget exhausted, then connection pool at capacity — the timeout was a symptom of waiting for a connection, not of Stripe being slow.
uc_ecom_outcome_line: Pool raised and the retry budget cut to two. Checkout error rate back to baseline within one evaluation window.
uc_ecom_cap_1_body: Set order.id on the span once and it is filterable everywhere spans are — the trace list, the error issue, the log search. No separate index to maintain.
uc_ecom_cap_2_body: The Stripe call is a client span with its own duration and status, so a third-party timeout is measured rather than inferred from your own error rate.
uc_ecom_cap_3_title: Logs are joined, not searched twice
uc_ecom_cap_3_body: The lines behind a span are reached from the span, not from a text query narrowed by hand to the same minute. That is the step that usually costs the most time.
uc_micro_seo_desc: Latency doubled with no deploy in sight. Follow one release across the service map, a trace and its logs to the connection pool that ran dry two hops away.
uc_micro_hero_lede: In a distributed system the service that got slow is rarely the service that broke. The map shows which edge degraded first, and the trace shows how far the wait propagated.
uc_micro_story_title: Two hops from the symptom to the cause
uc_micro_story_lede: payment-svc@1.4.2 is the release that shipped four hours before the symptom. It holds the path together — the map, the trace and the logs are all filtered to it.
uc_micro_step_1_title: The map shows a slow edge, not a slow service
uc_micro_step_1_body: api-gateway is the service being paged about, but its own spans are fine. The degraded edge is two hops in: payment-svc to user-db, average up from 12 ms to 210 ms.
uc_micro_step_2_title: The trace shows the wait, not the work
uc_micro_step_2_body: Open a slow request and the db span is almost all of it. The query itself is 4 ms; the span is 210 ms. The difference is time spent before the query ever ran.
uc_micro_step_3_body: Lines from that span read pool wait 206 ms, acquired after 3 attempts. Filter by service.version and they start at 1.4.2 — which raised concurrency without raising the pool.
uc_micro_outcome_line: Pool size raised to match the new concurrency. The p95 edge latency returned to 14 ms without a rollback.
uc_micro_cap_1_body: The map measures each caller-callee pair separately, so a dependency that degraded for one caller and not another is visible as one edge, not an average across the service.
uc_micro_cap_2_title: A db span is wait plus work
uc_micro_cap_2_body: Because the client span wraps acquisition as well as execution, pool starvation shows up as a gap between span duration and query duration instead of hiding inside a single number.
uc_micro_cap_3_title: No deploy is still a deploy
uc_micro_cap_3_body: service.version on every span means the question changes from who deployed to what version is this span from. A four-hour-old release is as findable as a four-minute-old one.
